54: Standing to assert the '142 Patent under Article III and 35 U.S.C. § 281; the court held NOV lacked standing because the Asset Contribution Agreement did not transfer the patent to it.
We agree with the district court that NOV lacks standing to assert the ’142 Patent because the agreement in question did not transfer the rights to the ’142 Patent to NOV.
183: Article III standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision: Phigenix lacked a concrete, particularized injury in fact and therefore lacked standing to appeal, so the appeal was dismissed.
Because Phigenix has not substantiated its alleged injury in fact, it lacks standing to appeal the PTAB’s Final Written Decision affirming the patentability of the Asserted Claims of the ’856 patent.
298: Standing to sue for breach of contract on the loan guarantee and second mortgage agreements; Lea lacked standing absent third-party beneficiary status, and the corporation's dissolution did not give him privity.

The only way Lea could have had standing to sue the government for breach of contract with regard to the loan guarantee agreement and the second mortgage agreement would have been, as we noted previously, if he were a third-party beneficiary to the contracts.
338: Standing for the Takings Clause claim: the complaint failed to allege an injury in fact, so the takings claim was dismissed.
the complaint failed to allege any "injury in fact," which is a prerequisite to establishing standing to bring a takings claim.
379: Whether the Government has standing to challenge the Claims Court's common fund attorney fee award; the court held the Government has an institutional interest and standing.

The Government possesses an institutional interest in assuring that courts do not abrogate Congress's intent by impermissibly substituting the common fund doctrine in place of a fee-shifting statute like the URA when awarding attorney fees.
398: Standing for the 35 U.S.C. § 256 inventorship claim based on reputational injury and resulting unemployment. The court held that concrete reputational injury can support Article III standing and that a genuine dispute of material fact existed, so summary judgment was vacated.
Today, we hold that concrete and particularized reputational injury can give rise to Article III standing.
399: Standing based on ownership and financial interest in the disputed patents. Bound by Filmtec, the court affirmed the district court's holding that the employment-agreement assignment left Shukh without an ownership or financial interest sufficient for standing.
As a panel, we are bound by Filmtec; we cannot overrule that holding without en banc action.
405: Standing to appeal a PTAB inter partes reexamination decision: the court held PPG had a particularized, concrete stake and standing to appeal.
We conclude that PPG did have standing to file this appeal, but that the controversy as to the patented subject matter is mooted by the Covenant Not To Sue.
441: Article III standing to assert a correction-of-inventorship claim under 35 U.S.C. § 256 (economic and reputational interests); district court dismissal affirmed.
We agree with the district court's conclusion that Ms. Huster lacked standing to assert that claim.
447: Standing under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(1): plaintiff failed to show direct economic interest (substantial chance of winning) as an interested party for unsolicited proposal bid protest
We hold that he did not possess the requisite interest and, thus, that Mr. Diaz has not satisfied his "burden of establishing the elements of standing."
516: Standing: whether BPV and Goldfarb had standing to sue for infringement of the '135 patent at the time of suit; court held law of the case bound it and plaintiffs had standing.
We are bound, therefore, by the prior panel's determination that the plaintiffs had standing and that the district court had jurisdiction.
588: Statutory standing under the false-marking statute, 35 U.S.C. § 292(b): whether Gravelle showed a competitive injury caused by Kaba's false 'patent pending' marking. Summary judgment affirmed for lack of injury.
Given the lack of concrete, non-speculative evidence of causation of an actual injury by Kaba's false marking, we affirm the entry of summary judgment for Kaba on Gravelle's false-marking claim.
589: Statutory standing under the Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a): whether Gravelle showed an economic or reputational injury proximately caused by the false advertising. Summary judgment affirmed.
We affirm the entry of summary judgment for Kaba on Gravelle's Lanham Act claim.
616: Standing to sue on the '581 patent: IV lacked standing because the Alset Agreement did not assign the '581 patent.
Because we conclude that the Alset Agreement did not convey any rights to the ’581 patent, IV lacked standing to bring suit on that patent.
702: Standing under 35 U.S.C. § 292(b) for a false marking claim: whether plaintiffs suffered a competitive injury; court held they lacked standing because they did not attempt to enter the market.
Accordingly, the district court properly granted summary judgment for Nautilus because Sukumar lacks standing to bring a claim for false marking under § 292.
740: Standing under 35 U.S.C. § 281: whether exclusive licensee Alps had standing to sue without joining patent owner AEI, given field-of-use restriction and nunc pro tunc amendment
Because Alps possessed neither legal title nor all substantial rights at the outset of this litigation, our standing jurisprudence required that Alps join the patent owner, AEI, as a co-plaintiff.
785: Standing: whether exclusive licensee Keranos held all substantial rights in the expired patents and could sue alone without joining the patent owner UMC
We agree with the district court that Keranos has standing to sue for infringement of the asserted patents.
788: Standing: whether CGI was an interested party (actual or prospective bidder with a direct economic interest) despite not submitting a bid.
Because CGI was a prospective bidder with a direct economic interest affected by the award of the contract, we conclude that CGI had standing to file its protest in the Court of Federal Claims.
802: Standing to sue for breach of contract: TriContinental, NOWIO-S and NOWIO-V lacked privity with the United States and so lacked standing.
In order to maintain a claim for breach of contract, a party must be in privity with the United States.
975: Statutory standing under AIA § 18(a)(1)(B): whether the Postal Service, as a defendant in a § 1498(a) suit, was 'sued for infringement' and so could petition for CBM review; the court held it was.
We therefore conclude that the Postal Service was 'sued for infringement' within the meaning of § 18(a)(1)(B) when Return Mail filed the Claims Court suit against it under § 1498(a).
1137: Standing of taxpayer to sue over alleged misuse of tax funds (breach of fiduciary duty claim)
Taxpayers lack standing to sue for alleged misuse of tax funds.
1272: Standing in a correction-of-inventorship action under 35 U.S.C. § 256: the district court dismissed for lack of standing, and the Federal Circuit reversed, so TriReme had standing to proceed.
TriReme appeals. We reverse and remand for further proceedings.
1483: Standing: whether Reoforce had Article III standing despite relinquishing its mining rights before suit; court reversed the Claims Court and held standing exists.
We conclude that Reoforce has standing to bring its suit here.
1519: Standing: whether WesternGeco owned the '607, '967 and '520 patents when suit was filed, and so had standing to assert them
There is thus substantial evidence to conclude that WesternGeco owns the patents at issue and has standing to sue.
1588: Standing: whether the Curtain Wall Coalition companies had standing as interested parties to request a scope ruling, as manufacturers or producers of a domestic like product.
1592: Standing: whether Starr has direct (not derivative) standing to pursue the equity-acquisition claims, which belong exclusively to AIG under Delaware law and third-party standing principles
we conclude that Starr and the shareholders represented by Starr lack standing to pursue the equity-acquisition claims directly, as those claims belong exclusively to AIG.
1754: Whether the VA had standing to file a motion to stay proceedings in the Veterans Court; the court held the VA, as a party, had the right to file such a motion.
We reject, moreover, Bell's assertion that the VA had no "standing" to file a motion to stay proceedings in the Veterans Court
1782: Standing of EFF, the PTAB petitioner, to defend the Board's decision on appeal; the court held Article III was satisfied as to the appellant and EFF was not excluded from defending the decision.
With Article III satisfied as to the appellant, EFF is not constitutionally excluded from appearing in court to defend the PTAB decision in its favor.
1802: Standing to seek a refund: the court held 8x8, a collector that passed the tax on to customers, lacks standing as a matter of law.
There is no genuine issue of material fact, and 8x8, a collector of the FCET, does not have standing as a matter of law to seek a refund of the FCET paid by its customers.
1811: Whether Agilent, a privy/claimed successor-in-interest rather than the third-party requester, has a statutory cause of action (standing) to appeal the inter partes reexamination decision under 35 U.S.C. §141; court held Agilent lacks cause of action and dismissed the appeal
For the foregoing reasons, we hold that Agilent lacks a statutory cause of action to appeal the reexamination decision to this court. Accordingly, we dismiss.
1876: Standing: Luminara, as exclusive licensee, held all substantial rights to the asserted patents and could sue without joining Disney Enterprises (patentee).
We hold that Luminara has all substantial rights to the patent and therefore it is not necessary to join Disney Enterprises in this lawsuit.
1920: Standing to sue the government on a contract claim: appellants lacked privity, agency, or third-party-beneficiary status, so they lack standing.

Because appellants are not in direct privity of contract with the government, fail to demonstrate an agency relationship, and do not qualify as third-party beneficiaries on the contract, appellants lack standing to sue the government on the contract claims asserted here.
2040: Whether the prevailing applicant retained a personal stake (Article III standing) to appeal the TTAB's decision; the court held he did not and dismissed the appeal.
We must dismiss the instant appeal because Mr. Beling has failed to meet his burden.
2276: Standing: whether Netzer, as assignee of the patent, had standing to sue despite the later name change
We therefore conclude that Netzer, as the owner of the ’496 patent as of January 24, 2014, has standing to maintain this action.
2318: Standing to sue for patent infringement: district court dismissed SPC for lack of standing because it did not obtain Ingenio's prior written consent required by the license agreement; Federal Circuit affirmed.
Thus, we affirm the district court's grant of the motion to dismiss for lack of standing.
2356: Article III standing for the section 256 correction of inventorship claim on the issued '637 patent; plaintiff lacked concrete reputational or economic injury

We affirm the district court's holding that Dr. Kamdem-Ouaffo lacked standing for his correction of inventorship claim because Dr. Kamdem-Ouaffo's sole claim of injury, in his Second Amended Complaint, stemming from his alleged loss of inventorship, was a bare assertion.
2379: Case or controversy (Article III standing and justiciability) for Apotex's declaratory-judgment action seeking a non-infringement judgment on a disclaimed patent; court held a justiciable controversy exists.

We conclude that "the facts alleged, under all the circumstances, show that there is a substantial controversy, between parties having adverse legal interests, of sufficient immediacy and reality to warrant the issuance of a declaratory judgment."
2604: Standing to object to the prize award under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b): the court held the contestant's contract was not a procurement contract, so Frankel lacked standing to bring a bid protest.

Therefore, we agree with the Court of Federal Claims that Mr. Frankel's contract with the FTC arising out of the Robocall Challenge was not a procurement contract and, consequently, Mr. Frankel did not have standing to register an objection to the prize award under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b).
2712: Standing to sue: Parrot argued Drone lacked standing because the assignor was not the true inventor; court held Drone had standing as successor in title and Article III injury.
We therefore affirm the district court’s denial of Parrot’s motion to dismiss for lack of standing without reviewing or endorsing the district court’s inventorship analysis.
2794: Whether Dourandish has standing to sue on the Quimba-Air Force contract as an intended third-party beneficiary, as a real party in interest, as a subcontractor-type privity party, or as a creditor beneficiary. The court held he lacks standing.
He has therefore not established that he was a third-party beneficiary to the contract between Quimba and the Air Force Research Laboratory.
2803: Constitutional standing to assert breach of the 1994 Helium Contract; the CFC's standing dismissal was held incorrect because the claim alleged economic injury.
Rocky Mountain met the constitutional standing requirement because it alleged a legally cognizable injury in fact that is "concrete and particularized"
3240: Whether the named Cobell plaintiffs lacked standing to assert the Fort Berthold claims so as to defeat the release; court found no standing problem
There is no standing issue that precludes application of the Cobell release to Appellants' Count I claims.
3249: Standing to appeal: the attorneys (interested party appellants sanctioned by the district court) lacked a redressable injury, so the court did not reach whether the sanctions order was a formal reprimand conferring standing.

Because we do not find we can redress the Attorneys' claimed injury, we need not decide whether the sanctions order in this case is the type of reprimand that could confer standing to pursue this appeal.
3295: Standing: whether plaintiff, as sole owner of an LLC, may sue on a contract made with the company, and whether he is a third-party beneficiary.
the Company and Mr. Ogunniyi are not legally identical entities (absent certain exceptions not implicated here).
3554: Real party in interest: whether GIT was the real party in interest after its bankruptcy transferred its claims to the secured creditors, so GIT lacked the right to prosecute the claims.
Based on the plain language of the documents involved in the bankruptcy proceedings, the answer is clearly yes.
3988: Article III standing: Lone Star adequately alleged exclusionary rights and infringement, so it has constitutional standing; whether it holds all substantial rights does not implicate standing or subject-matter jurisdiction.
Lone Star adequately alleged that it possesses exclusionary rights and that Appellees infringe those rights.
3995: Standing: whether Sally Perrie, having filed Chapter 7 bankruptcy, had standing to sue for correction of inventorship; the bankruptcy estate held the claim, so she lacked standing.
3996: Article III standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision upholding claims; the court held AVX lacked standing, rejecting both estoppel-based and competitor-standing theories.
Because we conclude that AVX lacks standing, we dismiss the appeal and do not reach the merits of the Board's ruling on the upheld claims.
4270: Real party in interest: whether the Pettinatis rather than BASR are the real parties in interest barring recovery of litigation costs; court held BASR is the beneficiary and the doctrine does not bar the award.
Accordingly, the real-party-in-interest doctrine, as applied in Unification Church, does not prevent BASR from obtaining an award under I.R.C. § 7430.
4303: Standing: Eskridge lacked standing as a bid protester because it lacked a direct economic interest (not an interested party under 28 U.S.C. §1491(b)(1)), no substantial chance of winning the contract.
Accordingly, because Eskridge failed to demonstrate a direct interest, it does not have standing to protest.
4345: Standing to assert the claims of the other fifteen consolidated plaintiffs: non-attorney Engle cannot represent them or rest his claim on their rights, so their claims were dismissed.
Engle is not an attorney, so he cannot represent these other plaintiffs. We therefore dismiss the claims of the other officers.
4366: Standing to petition to cancel a trademark registration before the TTAB: the court held Bank failed to plead a real interest and reasonable basis for belief of damage, so he lacked standing.
Accordingly, the TTAB properly determined that Mr. Bank lacked standing.
4406: Standing: Movants argued Uniloc lost constitutional standing after an alleged breach of the IBM agreement; the court rejected the argument and denied the motion to dismiss for lack of standing.
For the foregoing reasons, Movants motion to dismiss based on a loss of standing is denied.
4473: Standing to contest inventorship: Whitewater lacks standing to contest inventorship once the assignment is void
It follows from that holding, as Whitewater does not dispute, that Whitewater lacks standing to contest inventorship.
4629: Standing: whether intervenor attorneys have standing to pursue an EAJA attorney's fee claim over the prevailing veteran's objection, considering substantive rights, assignment, and third-party standing.
We conclude that the intervenors lack standing to pursue a claim for attorney's fees and affirm.
4678: Standing (entitlement to bring a cancellation proceeding under 15 U.S.C. § 1064): the Board held Australian lacked standing because it had contracted away its proprietary rights; the Federal Circuit held proprietary rights are not required and that Australian has a real interest and reasonable belief of damage, so standing exists.

We hold that a petitioner seeking to cancel a trademark registration establishes an entitlement to bring a cancellation proceeding under 15 U.S.C. § 1064 by demonstrating a real interest in the cancellation proceeding and a reasonable belief of damage regardless of whether petitioner lacks a proprietary interest in an asserted unregistered mark.
4761: Standing: whether surety GCNA had standing under the CDA to intervene and replace the contractor as appellant before the ASBCA; Board held it lacked standing because the claims arose before its takeover/settlement agreement, and the court affirmed.
Because all claims at issue here arose before GCNA entered into its settlement agreement with the Corps, GCNA could not assert them before the Board.
4823: Standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision: the petitioner-appellant did not establish an Article III injury in fact, so the appeal was dismissed.
Because JTEKT has failed to establish an actual injury sufficient to confer Article III standing, we dismiss this appeal.
4887: Standing: Frito-Lay, as cross-appellant from a refusal of registration, has standing to challenge the TTAB's finding of non-genericness.
Although the TTAB refused registration of Real Foods' proposed marks, Frito-Lay has standing to challenge the TTAB's finding of non-genericness
4997: Statutory standing: an individual claimant who does not represent a tribe or identifiable group of American Indians may not bring an Indian Tucker Act claim.
Ms. Cloud has not alleged that she is representing "a group of American Indians," and an individual may not bring such claims under § 1505.
5026: Standing to appeal the Board's final written decisions: the court independently found Samsung had Article III standing based on its royalty-pool injury.
We agree with Samsung that, under the facts and circumstances of this case, its injury confers Article III standing.
5105: Article III standing of an alleged sole inventor to bring a §256 correction-of-inventorship claim; district court had dismissed for lack of standing and the Federal Circuit found standing at the pleading stage.
In that case, Mr. James alleges that he is the sole inventor of the inventions claimed in the '638 patent... In the absence of other facts, that is enough to give Mr. James Article III standing.
5108: Standing of joined petitioners to appeal the Board's final written decision under 35 U.S.C. § 319 zone of interests
Accordingly, we conclude that Appellants fall within the zone of interests of § 319 and are not barred from appellate review.
5192: Standing of Jack Henry, as supplier and indemnitor, to participate in the declaratory judgment action despite PET's challenge; court held Jack Henry has standing.
Jack Henry, as supplier of the accused systems and as indemnitor of the Banks, has standing to participate in this action.
5225: Standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision: Momenta lacked Article III injury-in-fact after abandoning its biosimilar development, so it could not invoke appellate jurisdiction.
It is apparent that Momenta does not have standing to maintain this appeal in the federal courts.
5286: Standing to appeal a PTAB decision: court found Amerigen had Article III standing based on Orange Book listing blocking its ANDA launch, after UCB challenged standing.

We agree with Amerigen that it has standing to appeal from the Board's decision because the launch of its tentatively approved drug is blocked by the '650 patent, and invalidation of the patent would advance its drug's launch.
5288: Standing to appeal: Abboud, a non-party who was not sanctioned and against whom no judgment was entered, lacked Article III standing to appeal the contempt order.
Because there is no sanction against him and no injury, Abboud does not have standing to appeal.
5355: Standing: Jangho and Permasteelisa held to have Article III constitutional standing to challenge Commerce's scope ruling despite government's argument that the ruling concerned only Yuanda's merchandise.
Conducting the required inquiry, we conclude that Jangho and Permasteelisa have standing.
5418: Whether petitioner HVL sufficiently pled entitlement to seek cancellation under 15 U.S.C. 1064 (real interest and reasonable belief of damage), treated as a statutory cause of action rather than Article III standing
Accordingly, the Board did not err in concluding that HVL sufficiently pled entitlement to bring this cancellation proceeding.
5467: Article III standing to appeal the Commission's denial of a petition for rescission of a general exclusion order. The court held Mayborn had standing.
We agree with Mayborn that it has standing to appeal.
5549: Article III standing of the IPR petitioner to appeal the Board's final written decisions; court held Pfizer lacked standing at the outset and throughout the appeals, so the appeals were dismissed.

Because Pfizer has failed to establish that it was suffering a cognizable injury at all stages of these appeals sufficient to give Pfizer Article III standing to seek relief in this court, we dismiss the appeals.
5573: Standing to continue the interference: the Board held that Dionex lacks standing to continue the interference because its claims are indefinite and unpatentable, and the court affirmed.
Because the claims are indefinite and hence unpatentable, Dionex lacks standing to continue the interference.
5708: Standing to recover the deceased veteran's accrued benefits under 38 U.S.C. § 5121(a); the court held the son lacked standing.
Mr. Hiles does not have standing to recover the Veteran's accrued benefits under 38 U.S.C. § 5121(a).
5874: Article III standing: the court held Dollison failed to show a concrete and particularized injury in fact from the lack of a PTSD diagnosis, since ratings depend on symptoms and he showed no PTSD symptoms not also present in MDD, so the appeal was dismissed for lack of standing.
Therefore, we conclude that Dollison's unsubstantiated and hypothetical statements fail to demonstrate a concrete and particularized injury in fact.
5875: Standing to appeal the PTAB final written decision: petitioners (Google and LGE) held to have Article III standing based on infringement risk and collateral estoppel exposure.
We therefore conclude that Google and LGE have Article III standing to bring this appeal.
5887: Article III and statutory standing: majority held no standing defect existed because the complaint alleged ownership and infringement, treating the patentee requirement as non-jurisdictional under Lone Star.

Because Ms. Schwendimann's Complaint contained such allegations—that she is the owner by assignment of the '845 patent and Appellants infringed that patent—there is no "standing" issue to be decided in this appeal.
5898: Dismissal of treason and obstruction of justice claims for lack of standing because no private cause of action exists
Regarding the treason and obstruction of justice claims, the district court correctly determined that Dr. Arunachalam does not have standing to bring these claims.
5925: Standing: whether Appellants assigned their accrued breach of contract claims to the Government in the deeds in lieu of foreclosure, so as to lack a redressable injury on the contract claim.

Accordingly, because Appellants did not expressly or impliedly assign the Government their accrued claims for breach of contract based on the prepayment right, Appellants retain the legal right to pursue those claims and have established standing.
5937: Whether the USPTO Director, as intervenor with no appellee remaining, has Article III standing to defend the PTAB decision; majority found standing, Newman dissented.
The Director of the USPTO, thus, has standing.
5968: Standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision: Grit Energy, as petitioner, was found to have Article III standing based on the dismissed-without-prejudice infringement suit.
For the foregoing reasons, we conclude that Grit Energy has standing to pursue this appeal.
5974: Standing to appeal an IPR decision: the court held the IPR petitioner DuPont had Article III standing to appeal based on its operating demonstration plant and competitor status.
Under the circumstances here, we agree with DuPont that it has standing to appeal the Board's decision.
5978: Standing to appeal: whether Fitbit, as a joined party, has the right to appeal the Board's decision on claims 3-5 despite its petition not covering those claims
We hold that Fitbit has a right to appeal.
6049: Article III standing of the petitioner to appeal the Board's final written decision; the court held Argentum lacked standing because it showed no injury in fact, and dismissed the appeal without reaching the merits.
Accordingly, we hold that Argentum has failed to prove that it has suffered an injury in fact necessary to establish standing.
6065: Article III standing of the petitioner to appeal the PTAB final written decision in post-grant review; court found injury in fact based on imminent infringement threat and estoppel effect.
Therefore, considering these factors collectively, we hold that Altaire has demonstrated injury in fact, such that it has standing to challenge the PTAB's Final Written Decision.
6234: Standing: Acetris lacked standing to challenge the Entecavir solicitation because it was the highest-price bidder, but had constitutional and statutory standing for its challenge to future procurements.
Thus, Acetris does not now have standing to challenge the Entecavir solicitation.
6325: Standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision: GE lacked Article III injury in fact, so appeal dismissed.
We hold that GE lacks Article III standing to appeal the Board's Final Written Decision and therefore dismiss the appeal.
6342: Associational standing of NOVA to challenge the Knee Joint Stability Rule and Knee Replacement Rule based on veteran members
NOVA has sufficiently shown that it has associational standing to challenge the Knee Joint Stability Rule and the Knee Replacement Rule.
6486: Whether Schirripa has standing as an 'interested party' to bring a bid protest under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(1); held he is not an interested party.
As discussed supra, these statutes have no relation to any contract theory or any government bid or procurement practice.
6580: Article III standing: the Tribe failed to allege an injury in fact to its Winters water rights, so the Claims Court's dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction was affirmed.
We affirm, concluding that the Tribe has failed to establish, or even allege, that it has suffered the requisite injury in fact.
6628: Standing: whether Advanced Video had standing to sue for infringement of the '788 patent without co-owner Hsiun as a party, given that it did not hold full title.

Advanced Video does not have full ownership of the '788 patent. Ms. Hsiun is neither a party to the suits, nor has she consented to these suits. Advanced Video, therefore, has no standing to maintain its suit.
6658: Eligibility to be substituted as claimant after veteran's death (standing to pursue accrued benefits claim), decided as the substitution-eligibility question

We affirm the decision of the Veterans Court denying Mr. Sucic's adult children's motion for substitution because they are not eligible accrued benefits beneficiaries under 38 U.S.C. § 5121(a)(2)(B) as "[t]he veteran's children" as properly construed.
6889: Statutory standing to appeal to the Board: the court read claimant in 38 U.S.C. 7105(b)(2)(A) to include legal entities such as Ashford, so Ashford may appeal a VA suspension or discontinuance decision to the Board.
Thus, we read 'claimant' in 38 U.S.C. § 7105(b)(2)(A) to include legal entities like Ashford.
7054: Statutory standing to appeal: whether NMGGC, whose review request was declared illegitimate, was a party to the administrative proceeding entitled to contest the final results under 19 U.S.C. 1516a and 28 U.S.C. 2631(c)
Thus, NMGGC was not a 'party to the proceeding.'
7089: Standing to appeal: Surti cannot appeal the judgment against Mudguard on the tortious interference claim because Mudguard is not an appellant, so that judgment stands.
Mr. Surti cannot appeal on behalf of Mudguard. Thus, the judgment against Mudguard must stand.
7132: Standing to bring a pre-award bid protest: the court found ARC had standing as a prospective bidder with a non-trivial competitive injury, separate from the merits.

we agree with ARC that having to compete for the 2018 RFQ on an unrestricted basis is a "non-trivial competitive injury" capable of being redressed by this court, and we find that ARC has standing to bring its pre-award protest.
7215: Standing to bring a bid protest: the Court of Federal Claims dismissed for lack of standing because CliniComp, an incumbent, could not show it was a qualified bidder who would have had a substantial chance of receiving the sole-source contract, so it lacked a direct economic interest and prejudice.
We therefore conclude that CliniComp lacks standing in this bid protest.
7257: Standing: whether Uniloc or Uniloc 2017 held enforceable title and standing to sue at the inception of the suit. The court left the question for the district court in the first instance, noting Apple has a basis to contest standing.

We remand this case to the district court for the purpose of supplementing the record with the documents pertaining to jurisdiction and resolving the presented jurisdictional issues in the first instance.
7351: Whether tribal sovereign immunity can be asserted to bar an IPR proceeding (threshold defense to Board authority to proceed; Board denied termination and withdrawal).
We hold that tribal sovereign immunity cannot be asserted in IPRs.
7364: Standing to appeal PTAB final written decision: Adidas had Article III standing despite no infringement suit threatened against it
We therefore conclude that Adidas has Article III standing to bring this appeal.
7419: Whether SFM was entitled under 15 U.S.C. § 1064 to bring and maintain a cancellation petition (statutory cause of action under Lexmark zone-of-interests and proximate-causation framework); court framed it as statutory entitlement rather than Article III standing.
We therefore hold that the Board correctly determined that SFM falls within the class of parties whom Congress has authorized to sue under the statutory cause of action of § 1064.
7440: Article III standing of petitioner Choirock to appeal the Board's final written decision; court rejected Spin Master's challenge and found standing.
We reject Spin Master's contention that Choirock lacks Article III standing to prosecute this appeal.
7456: Whether the § 262 co-owner joinder requirement is a jurisdictional Article III standing defect; court held it is a non-jurisdictional statutory prerequisite, not Article III standing.

AntennaSys's failure to join Windmill as a co-plaintiff impacts AntennaSys's ability to satisfy the statutory prerequisites for bringing an infringement suit; it does not impact AntennaSys's Article III standing.
7478: Article III and antitrust standing: Golden's antitrust claims dismissed for lack of Article III and antitrust injury/standing.

We agree with the district court that Mr. Golden's vague, conclusory allegations as to antitrust violations (without specifically identifying the supposed illegal conduct) and allegations of injury (again without specifying the specific injury) are not adequate to allege either Article III standing or antitrust injury.
7564: Antitrust injury and antitrust standing: Golden is not alleged to be a participant in the same market as Qualcomm and did not plead antitrust injury; antitrust claim dismissed.
We thus agree with the district court that Golden has failed to plausibly plead an antitrust claim.
7617: Standing: L'Oreal argued Liqwd and Olaplex LLC lost standing after transferring patent interests, mooting the appeal; court held standing existed when the notice of appeal was filed.
It is uncontested that Liqwd and Olaplex LLC had standing when the permanent injunction was entered and when their notice of appeal was filed, which is when our jurisdiction attached.
7665: Article III standing to appeal: Sebela lacked constitutional standing to appeal because the district court's invalidity holding rested only on obviousness, which Sebela did not challenge; appeal dismissed.
we conclude Sebela lacks constitutional standing to bring this appeal.
7796: Standing: whether Omni has an exclusionary right in the asserted patents given UM bylaw 3.10 (whether paragraph 1 effected a present automatic assignment to UM); court held Omni is assignee and has standing.

We agree with the Eastern District of Texas that paragraph 1 of bylaw 3.10 does not presently automatically assign Dr. Islam's rights to the patent but rather, at most, "reflects a future agreement to assign rather than a present assignment."
7859: Standing: whether SEKRI, a mandatory source under the AbilityOne Program, qualifies as an actual or prospective bidder and interested party under 28 U.S.C. 1491(b)(1).
We hold that SEKRI qualifies as a prospective bidder for standing purposes because DLA was aware during the bidding process that SEKRI is a mandatory source of ATAP in the AbilityOne Program.
7922: Standing of Schiedmayer Celesta to bring the cancellation proceeding under the false association bar; Sweet 16's challenge was rejected.
To the extent Sweet 16 is arguing that Schiedmayer Celesta lacked standing to bring the cancellation proceeding, the Board correctly rejected that argument.
7967: Standing to appeal the PTAB decision; the court found LKQ had standing based on its substantial risk of infringement.
LKQ is therefore currently engaged in conduct creating a substantial risk of infringement, and we find that it has standing to appeal.
8019: Standing to appeal: whether Shamoon, a nonparty who sought substitution, was aggrieved and could appeal the denial of substitution after dismissal; the court found he had standing.

Mr. Shamoon was aggrieved by the district court's order that denied his motion to substitute himself for Ubiquitous as the plaintiff upon the grant of the motion for dismissal of the case without prejudice.
8057: Standing: direct takings and illegal exaction claims are substantively derivative under Delaware/federal law, so shareholders lack standing to bring them directly
We conclude that, though directly styled, shareholders' claims are substantively derivative under Delaware law.
8059: Cacciapalle lacked privity of contract with the United States for his stock-certificate contract claim
We, thus, affirm the Claims Court's decision to dismiss these claims on standing (privity) grounds.
8110: Article III standing of Intel to appeal the Board's final written decision, challenged by Qualcomm; court found standing.
We therefore find that Intel has standing and proceed to consider the merits of its appeal.
8111: Standing to appeal the RO's apportionment denial to the Board: the court held Akard, a veteran rather than the potential apportionment recipient, could not appeal under 38 U.S.C. § 7105(b)(2) and the Veterans Court's 'personal stake' language was read as resting on that statutory limit.
We see no legal error in that ruling.
8118: Standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision: Intuitive, no longer a party after estoppel, lacked statutory standing under 35 U.S.C. 141(c) and 319 to appeal the merits decision.

Once § 315(e)(1) prohibited Intuitive from maintaining this IPR, Intuitive ceased to be a party under § 141 and § 319, placing it outside the zone of interest established by the congressionally authorized right to appeal in those provisions.
8124: Constitutional Article III standing: court held USFRF had at least one exclusionary right, so constitutional standing was satisfied and the district court's contrary dismissal was clearly erroneous.
we hold USFRF fails to meet the statutory requirements of § 281 but does meet the requirements of constitutional standing.
8151: Standing to appeal the PTAB final written decisions: Qualcomm contested Intel's standing, and the court found Intel had a non-speculative risk of being sued and therefore standing.
As such, Intel has demonstrated a non-speculative risk of being sued by Qualcomm for infringement and therefore has standing to bring this appeal.
8163: Article III and statutory standing to appeal: applicant lacked standing to appeal a Board decision dismissing the opposition in its favor, so the court lacked jurisdiction.
Because dismissal was in Appellant’s favor, Appellant lacks standing to appeal, and we lack jurisdiction.
8197: Standing: district court dismissed for lack of standing; affirmed on basis that dismissal is without prejudice
On this basis, we affirm the district court's decision to dismiss this case for lack of standing.
8199: Standing to bring the rulemaking challenges under 38 U.S.C. § 502: associational standing found for PVA and MVA on three challenges (§ 14.636(c)(1)(i), § 3.2500(b), § 3.155); no standing found for the remaining challenges.

We conclude that two veterans' service organizations, MVA and PVA, have demonstrated associational standing based on claimed injuries to their members to collectively bring three of their seven challenges.
8260: Standing to appeal the Board's final written decision: Intel was held to have Article III standing based on Qualcomm's prior infringement suit against Apple accusing an Intel product and its ongoing risk of suit.
Because Intel's risks transcend mere conjecture or hypothesis, see Spokeo, 578 U.S. at 339, we conclude that Intel has standing.
8488: Standing to appeal: whether Target, a nonparty to the CIT action whose motion to intervene was denied as moot, may appeal as a nonparty; the court held no exceptional circumstances warrant a nonparty appeal and dismissed.
Target has not established exceptional circumstances indicating the propriety of a nonparty appeal in this case. Accordingly, we dismiss.
8490: Standing of proposed intervenors to intervene (piggyback standing and independent standing) in the CIT Section 232 exclusion cases; the court held the intervenors established piggyback standing in all six cases, reversing the CIT's contrary standing determination.
Because in each of these cases the proposed intervenors' requested relief is largely identical to the government's prayer for relief, the proposed intervenors have established piggyback standing.
8532: Standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision: appellant Allgenesis failed to show an Article III injury in fact based on potential infringement liability or the Board's priority determination.
For these reasons, we conclude Allgenesis has failed to establish an injury in fact sufficient to confer Article III standing.
8533: Standing to assert infringement: the court held Sgromo lacked ownership of the asserted patents and trademarks when he sued, so he lacked standing.
Because Sgromo lacked ownership of the patents and trademarks at issue when he brought this suit, he lacks standing to assert his claims for infringement.
8757: Standing to appeal the PTAB final written decision; court found GE had Article III standing based on concrete plans creating substantial risk of future infringement.
GE has alleged sufficient facts to establish that it is engaging in activity that creates a substantial risk of future infringement, GE has standing to bring its appeal.
8808: Organizational (associational) standing of MVA to challenge the Blue Water Navy Rule and other M21-1 provisions; the court rejected the Secretary's standing objection.
Having reviewed the record, we do not agree with the Secretary that the MVA lacks organizational standing here.
8826: Standing to appeal: patent owner BMI lacked Article III standing to appeal the unpatentability determination for claim 1 because it had finally canceled the claim before filing its notice of appeal; collateral estoppel injury rejected.
BMI therefore lacks standing to appeal the Board's patentability determination for claim 1, and we lack jurisdiction over this part of BMI's appeal.
9128: Standing: whether Reuben, a non-signatory company chairman, had third-party beneficiary standing to sue on the Army license agreement; the court held he lacked standing and dismissed him.
Reuben has not made such a showing.
9182: Associational standing of Veteran Warriors to challenge the 'three or more activities of daily living' pathway in the 'unable to self-sustain' definition; no member had standing, so the challenge was dismissed.
Thus, we dismiss Petitioners' challenge to the "three or more activities of daily living" requirement for a veteran to qualify as unable to self-sustain in the community.
9183: Standing established for the remaining challenges, through declarants and members who were denied benefits under the challenged provisions.
Thus, Veteran Warriors has proven all three prongs of associational standing for these challenges.
9213: Standing: plaintiffs, as individual Osage headright owners, have standing to bring breach of trust claims because the 1906 Act creates a trust relationship with them; Claims Court dismissal for lack of standing reversed.
We find that, under the 1906 Act, such a trust relationship exists and plaintiffs have standing.
9242: Standing under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(1): whether the losing bidder HVF West was an interested party with a substantial chance of winning the award, given its failure to challenge the eligibility of the price-superior bidders.
Because we hold that HVF lacks standing to bring the protest, we reverse on that ground and do not reach the other grounds for reversal argued by Lamb and the Government.
9253: Standing to bring a bid protest under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(1): the court held Asset was an ineligible bidder because its non-responsive proposal gave it no substantial chance of winning, so it lacked standing.

Thus, because of the error in Asset's bid, Asset was an ineligible bidder, did not have a substantial chance of winning the ICE contract, and was without standing to challenge ICE's award of the contract to Akima.
9284: Standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision in an IPR; court found Moderna had standing based on risk of infringement suit.
we conclude that Moderna has standing to pursue its appeal based on the risk of an infringement suit, and we proceed to the merits of this appeal.
9384: Standing: whether the Termination Agreement eliminated Fortress's license, restoring Uniloc 2017's right to exclude and standing to sue
We therefore reverse the district court and remand this case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.
9396: Standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision: Apple failed to establish Article III injury in fact from ongoing payment obligations, possible future infringement suits, or §315(e) estoppel, so the appeals were dismissed.
Because we hold Apple has failed to establish standing, we dismiss.
9432: Appellate standing of AMD to cross-appeal Board's unpatentability determinations on claims Polaris did not assert in district court; standing found.
We conclude, therefore, that AMD has standing to bring its cross-appeal.
9575: Article III standing of an IPR petitioner to appeal PTAB final written decisions after settlement and a global license; court held Apple lacked standing, following Apple I.
Per Apple I, therefore, we dismiss for lack of standing.
9676: Whether the shareholders have standing to assert their substantively derivative claims as direct claims.
The Washington Federal Plaintiffs lack standing to assert their substantively derivative claim as a direct takings claim.
9690: Appellate standing: the prevailing party in the district court cannot seek appellate relief from the transfer order, so the appeal was dismissed (prudential rule).
Regardless, because Ms. Armstrong prevailed below, we dismiss her appeal of the district court's transfer order.
9811: Claim based on the Air Force's future alleged infringement of the '408 patent dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because the alleged future injury was conjectural or hypothetical.
that alleged future injury is "conjectural or hypothetical."
9812: Article III standing to appeal the Board's unpatentability determination for claim 1, which BMI had finally canceled before filing its notice of appeal; collateral estoppel injury held insufficient.
BMI therefore lacks standing to appeal the Board's patentability determination for claim 1, and we lack jurisdiction over this part of BMI's appeal.
9890: Standing to bring bid protest: whether protester had substantial chance of winning award (interested party under 28 U.S.C. §1491(b)(1))
We therefore hold that the Court of Federal Claims erred when it dismissed VAS's protest for lack of standing.
9896: Whether the sole proprietorship SES may sue separately from its owner; held SES has no separate legal identity, so Siegler is the only plaintiff.
We also agree with the district court that the only plaintiff in this action is Siegler.
9924: Article III standing of petitioner BASF to appeal the PTAB final written decision in a PGR; court found standing based on planned U.S. sales and prior infringement suit by Ingevity.
we conclude that BASF has satisfied the requirements for Article III standing.
10110: Article III standing: whether WiNet owned the '374 patent and thus had standing when it filed suit. The court found a serious question and vacated for the district court to decide standing in the first instance, without deciding it.
The record now before us creates a serious question about WiNet's Article III standing.
10141: Statutory cause of action under Lanham Act 14(3): Coca-Cola failed to show lost U.S. sales as the injury needed for statutory standing to cancel the registrations.
Coca-Cola did not establish damage from lost sales.
10142: Statutory cause of action under Lanham Act 14(3): Coca-Cola failed to show reputational injury in the United States, because substantial evidence did not support the Board's finding that the marks' reputation extended to the U.S.
We hold that substantial evidence does not support the Board's finding that the reputations of Coca-Cola's THUMS UP and LIMCA marks extend to the United States.
10212: Capacity to sue and real party in interest / standing of the five entities doing business as Red Sun Farms; remanded for Trade Court to address, no decision reached
On remand, the Trade Court should address issues raised by the naming of "Red Sun Farms" as the lone "Plaintiff" in the caption of the case.
10263: Standing to appeal the Board's IPR decision: the court held Moderna lacked Article III standing when it filed the appeal and failed to show continuous standing, so its appeal was dismissed.
We agree with Arbutus that Moderna lacked standing at the time the appeal was filed.
10405: Whether StrongVolt had a real interest and statutory entitlement to petition to cancel, including whether its later dissolution defeated that interest
We have long held that rejection of an application to register one's own trademark based on a likelihood of confusion with a registered mark demonstrates a real interest.
10545: Standing: Land Shark had a substantial chance of receiving the contract as the lowest bidder and so had direct economic interest and standing to protest the solicitation withdrawal under the Tucker Act.

Because Land Shark had a substantial chance of receiving the contract as the lowest bidder on the SDVOSB set-aside solicitation but for alleged errors, we conclude that Land Shark had standing to protest the withdrawal of the solicitation and proceed to the merits.
10803: Article III standing: the court held that Uniloc lacked standing to sue for infringement because it granted Fortress a license with the right to sublicense, which Uniloc is collaterally estopped from contesting.
We hold that, in light of Apple 2020 WL 7122617, Uniloc is collaterally estopped from asserting that it has standing in these cases.
10848: Standing: at least Apple has Article III standing to press the notice-and-comment rulemaking challenge to the Director's instructions.
We also conclude that at least Apple has standing to press the challenge to the Director’s instructions as invalid for want of notice-and-comment rulemaking.
11063: Article III standing to appeal the Board's dismissal of the opposition as to Class 5 sanitizing preparations; Brewery lacked standing, so the appeal was dismissed.
Because Brewery lacks Article III standing to oppose the '776 Application as to the sanitizing preparations under Class 5, we dismiss its appeal as to those goods.
11064: Article III standing to challenge the existing and applied-for marks for Class 32 beer-making kits; standing was found.
This is sufficient to establish Brewery's standing to challenge the existing and applied-for marks for beer-making kits.
11131: Standing to appeal an arbitrator's denial of attorney fees: the union lacked statutory standing under 5 U.S.C. 7703(a)(1) and Reid, and failed the first Hunt associational-standing prong.
Because AFGE does not have standing to appeal that denial, we dismiss this appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
11198: Standing: the local union lacked statutory standing under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(a) to appeal the arbitration award, and the parties did not dispute that.
Here, in contrast, the local Union does not have standing by operation of the statute, 5 U.S.C. § 7703(a).
11269: Statutory standing as an interested party under 28 U.S.C. 1491(b)(1): protester not shown to have a substantial chance of winning the contract after 'Not Selectable' classification
However, she fails to show she "had a substantial chance of winning the contract" given her proposal's "Not Selectable" classification.
11311: Article III standing: Causam must show ownership of the '268 patent by evidence to establish injury in fact; the court held Causam has standing because it owns the patent.
Thus, Causam has carried its burden to show Article III standing.
11411: Statutory cause of action / standing under 15 U.S.C. § 1064 for cancellation petitioner Narita Export; court held petitioner had a real interest and reasonable belief in damage, and rejected Adaptrend's forfeiture argument on the merits.
We conclude that the Board correctly determined that Narita Export is entitled to a statutory cause of action under § 1064.
11422: Article III standing to appeal the Board's unpatentability ruling based on Causam's ownership of the '268 patent; court found Causam has standing.
Causam thus has standing to appeal the Board's unpatentability ruling, which, if it becomes final, will lead to cancellation of all claims of the '268 patent but claim 12
11423: Third-party standing: Causam lacks standing to assert the due process notice rights of the claimed true owner of the patent.
The right to assert that due process violation, however, does not belong to Causam, but to whoever might be the claimed true owner of the '268 patent.
11493: Whether the exclusive licensee holds all substantial rights so as to have standing to sue alone without joining the patent owner; court held it does.
Accordingly, we hold that the Agreement granted TexasLDPC all substantial rights, and the district court's contrary finding cannot sustain a Rule 12(b)(7) dismissal.
11515: Standing: the appellant lacked a personal stake in the appeal because any patent issuing from the application would have zero term and no exclusionary rights; the court dismissed for lack of personal interest.
Mr. Forest has identified no potential interest other than receiving a patent with the patent rights afforded by section 154.
11579: Organizational standing of IRAdvocates to challenge CBP's inaction on its section 307 petitions; the court held no injury-in-fact (expenditure of resources and denial of procedural right insufficient).
we hold that IRAdvocates has not established that it suffered a concrete injury and thus that it has standing to challenge Customs' inaction in response to its petitions.
11700: Standing to appeal: a non-party to the Board proceedings may not appeal the adverse judgment on his own behalf.
[t]he rule that only parties to a lawsuit, or those that properly become parties, may appeal an adverse judgment, is well settled.
11703: Statutory standing: Utech was not an interested party under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(1) because it neither bid nor was a prospective bidder before the proposal deadline, so it lacked standing to assert Counts II and III.
The Court of Federal Claims did not err in its determination that Utech was not an "interested party."
11726: Sherman's standing to appeal the correction of inventorship claim, where the nonparty did not intervene or substitute and Cooper did not appeal; appeal dismissed.
we conclude that Sherman does not have the right to appeal the correction of inventorship claim.
11747: Standing to appeal: the court agreed that Sandstrom, as assignee of the asserted patents, established standing to pursue the appeal.
We agree with the Commission that Sandstrom has established standing to pursue his appeal.
11771: Article III standing: Asus argued Lone Star lacked standing for failure to prove written evidence of ownership; court held Article III standing satisfied based on unrebutted testimony, while statutory standing argument was forfeited.
Lone Star has satisfied Article III standing.
11843: Standing: Article III standing of the sole proprietorship to bring the bid protest; no redressable injury because both the proprietorship and MGI were debarred
Accordingly, even if Ms. Monbo could show an injury-in-fact sufficient to support Article III standing, she has failed to present a redressable injury.
12111: Article III standing: the court held the complaint inadequately alleged the Nesarikars' ownership of, and concrete interest in, the '288 application, so dismissal without prejudice for lack of standing was affirmed.
we agree with the district court that Nesarikars have no such interest in the ’288 application.
12266: Whether the Board had jurisdiction over the IRA appeal given failure to exhaust OSC remedies for protected disclosures (standing/jurisdictional threshold for IRA appeal)
we see no error in Board's determination that Mr. Owens did not exhaust administrative remedies before the OSC as to any disclosures beyond the racial discrimination claim.
12425: Standing: whether Oak Grove is an interested party prejudiced by the procurement errors. Court found standing.
Thus, Oak Grove had standing to challenge the awardability of F3EA and Lukos.
12474: Standing: Claims Court held Monbo lacked constitutional and statutory standing to bring bid protests because of her debarment.
The Claims Court dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because Ms. Monbo's debarment meant that she lacked constitutional standing and statutory standing.
12536: Article III standing: Hyatt lacked standing to pursue §145 claims for pending claims the Board reversed, so the district court lacked jurisdiction over them.
Based on this record, Mr. Hyatt does not have standing under Article III to bring a § 145 action as to the pending claims for which the Board reversed the examiner's rejections.
12542: Standing to appeal the Board's dismissal of the cancellation petition: the court held Messier lacked Article III standing because he alleged no concrete, particularized injury from the Saints mark, so it lacked jurisdiction to reach the merits.
Because Mr. Messier lacks standing to bring this appeal, we dismiss.
12622: Standing: organizational and associational standing to seek injunctive and declaratory relief against the PTO's patent cover language; the court held appellant organizations and members lacked standing.
Appellants have not adequately pleaded a threat of future injury from the conduct that they challenge. They have therefore failed to establish standing to seek injunctive and declaratory relief.
12714: Standing: whether Percipient, a non-bidder that did not bid on the SAFFIRE contract, is an interested party under 28 U.S.C. 1491(b)(1) able to bring a bid protest based on an alleged violation of 10 U.S.C. 3453. En banc court held an interested party must be an actual or prospective bidder or offeror whose direct economic interest would be affected by the award or failure to award, regardless of the type of challenge, and affirmed dismissal for lack of standing.

We conclude that an 'interested party' who has standing to bring a bid protest under § 1491(b) is an actual or prospective bidder or offeror whose direct economic interest would be affected by the award of the contract or by failure to award the contract, regardless of the type of challenge brought. We therefore affirm the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal of Percipient's protest for lack of standing.
12724: Article III standing to appeal a PTAB PGR final written decision: Incyte failed to show injury in fact based on potential infringement liability or competitor standing, so the appeal was dismissed.
Because Incyte fails to establish an injury in fact sufficient to confer Article III standing, we dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
12760: Standing to appeal: whether the claimants had an injury redressable by the Federal Circuit after the Board's post-NOA actions gave them the relief they sought; court held they lack standing.
For the reasons stated below, the claimants lack standing to pursue these appeals before this court. We therefore lack jurisdiction and, accordingly, dismiss.
12885: Statutory standing (Lexmark zone-of-interests and proximate cause) to oppose registration under 15 U.S.C. § 1063; Board held opposer, a mere consumer, was not entitled to oppose on descriptiveness, genericness and failure-to-function grounds, and affirmed.
Because the Board correctly applied the Lexmark framework to find that Ms. Curtin did not have statutory standing to oppose UTH's registration of the RAPUNZEL mark under § 1063, we affirm.
12886: Standing: Veterans Court erred in its standing analysis; petitioners had standing at the time the petition was filed, so the standing ruling is vacated.
The Veterans Court erred in its standing analysis and abused its discretion in determining that the commonality and adequacy requirements of Rule 23 were not met.
12973: Standing based on indemnification liability: Mitek failed to show a reasonable potential for indemnification liability to its customers, given carve-outs in the indemnification agreements and the broken indemnification chain.
We reject Mitek's attempt to establish standing based on the existence of these agreements alone.
13011: Article III standing to appeal the PTAB final written decision, including standing based on 35 U.S.C. § 319, the § 312(a)(2) RPI informational right, and asserted harms from the unadjudicated RPI dispute. Court held Dolby lacked standing and dismissed.
Because Dolby fails to establish an injury in fact sufficient to confer standing to appeal, we dismiss.
13083: Article III standing to appeal a PGR final written decision; the court held appellant ironSource failed to show injury in fact based on potential infringement liability, so the appeal was dismissed.
Because ironSource fails to establish an injury in fact sufficient to confer standing to appeal, we dismiss.
13127: Standing: whether AIT had constitutional standing (exclusionary patent rights at inception of suit) given the 2006 Agreement transferred patent rights to Nelson before the 2012 Assignment to AIT
AIT therefore had no exclusionary patent rights at the inception of the lawsuit and lacked constitutional standing to sue under them.
13132: Standing to petition for review of VA rules under 38 U.S.C. 502; court found the Lathams have standing as legacy participants subject to the rule.
While the Lathams have standing to challenge the VA regulations, their contentions fail on the merits.
13201: Statutory standing (interested party under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(1)) to challenge the award of a SeaPort-NxG MAC to Precise; Island Creek was a successful awardee, not a disappointed bidder, so it lacked standing.
To the extent Count IV challenges the IDIQ contract award to Precise, Island Creek lacks statutory standing to challenge this award.
13239: Article III standing: whether IT (patent owner) retained at least one exclusionary right in the '247 patent despite Main Street's non-exclusive licensing ability and option to assign upon default; the court held IT had injury-in-fact standing and reversed the dismissal.
The answer is a clear yes.
13276: Article III standing of petitioner CSI to pursue cross-appeal of Board's nonobviousness ruling on claim 5; court found standing
CSI has sufficiently shown that it is engaging in activity that creates a substantial risk of future infringement.
13342: Standing to appeal an ITC termination: Koki failed to show an injury in fact sufficient to confer standing to appeal.
Koki has failed to meet its burden to establish standing.
13374: Whether Apple has statutory standing to appeal the Board's decision despite Gesture's argument that 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(1) estoppel bars the appeal; court treated Apple as having standing.
we agree with Apple that Gesture's argument that Apple is a real party in interest or privy of Unified Patents was forfeited.
13470: Standing: VDPP lacks standing to contest sanctions imposed on its counsel Mr. Ramey
VDPP has suffered no injury from Mr. Ramey's sanctions and, in fact, benefited from his sanctions
13589: Article III constitutional standing to appeal the Board's dismissal: the appellant showed injury in fact, causation and redressability through its ownership interest in Hobbs Winery.
We are therefore satisfied that Appellant has met its burden as to Article III standing in this case and can therefore proceed to the merits.
13590: Statutory entitlement to seek cancellation under 15 U.S.C. § 1064 (Lexmark zone of interests and proximate causation): the minority partner lacked a commercial interest and its injury was too remote, so it had no statutory cause of action.
we conclude that it is not within the zone of interests entitled to seek cancellation of those marks under § 1064.
13646: Standing to seek review of the MSPB decision as a non-employee, non-applicant petitioner; constitutional standing not reached
Because we determine that Mr. Dowling lacks a statutory right to petition for review, we do not reach the issue of constitutional standing.
13695: Standing: plaintiff (notice partner North Hills) lacked Article III standing because it failed to identify or prove a redressable injury; burden on party invoking jurisdiction.
At least by the time the Court of Federal Claims dismissed the case, North Hills lacked standing because it failed to identify—let alone adequately prove—the existence of a redressable injury.
13849: Article III standing to appeal the Board's final written decision; court found Streck had standing based on Ravgen's infringement accusations and suits against customers.

The claim charts and accompanying statements filed with the Board, coupled with Ravgen's history of filing infringement suits against Streck's customers, establish the risk of an infringement suit against Streck sufficient to grant standing to appeal a final written decision of the Board.
13919: Standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision: petitioner failed to show injury in fact based on potential infringement liability.
Because PTOT has failed to establish an injury in fact sufficient to confer standing to appeal, we dismiss.
14189: Standing: Mid Continent's Article III and statutory standing to pursue the interlocutory appeal of the injunction.
We conclude that Mid Continent has Article III standing as well as "statutory" standing.
14258: Standing to appeal the denial of a mandatory stay: Ascendis, as ITC respondent and declaratory-judgment plaintiff, showed a controversy of sufficient immediacy and reality because BioMarin could seek to lift the discretionary stay and pursue a preliminary injunction upon FDA approval.
we hold that Ascendis has demonstrated a controversy of sufficient immediacy and reality to satisfy Article III standing.
14297: Standing of Cotter as an intended third-party beneficiary to sue on the Indemnification Agreement; Claims Court's lack-of-standing dismissal reversed and standing found at the pleading stage.
We reverse the district court’s conclusion of lack of standing, which rested on the court’s error on the statutory entitlement question.
14335: Statutory standing as an interested party under prong three of 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(1) for a prospective offeror of commercial items alleging § 3453 violations; held Percipient has standing.
Under these facts, we hold that Percipient has standing to challenge the agency's alleged violation of § 3453.
14349: Standing: SBA retaliation claim concerned an EIDL application by AI Net Group LLC, not Aljindi individually, so the pro se plaintiff could not pursue it on the LLC's behalf.
the SBA's action regarding the requested EIDL was directed at AI Net Group LLC and thus his claim is "on behalf of AI Net Group LLC, not Dr. Aljindi as an individual."
14359: Fact-finding challenge: alleged impermissible factfinding by Veterans Court; court found no factfinding and no basis to reverse.
We do not see the Veterans Court as having engaged in fact finding, either in the portion of its opinion emphasized by Mr. Champagne or anywhere else.
14500: Standing to appeal to the Federal Circuit: both claimants lacked standing because the Board's post-NOA actions gave them all the relief they sought, so no effectual relief remained.
For the reasons stated below, the claimants lack standing to pursue these appeals before this court.
14518: Standing of Syngenta to appeal denial of sanctions motion
we conclude that, under Article III of the Constitution and its established injury-causation-redressability requirement, Syngenta has standing to seek review of the denial of standing.
14553: Article III constitutional standing: whether Medtronic Ireland retained an exclusionary right after licensing rights to Medtronic Galway; the court held it did and reversed the dismissal of the counterclaims.
Because Medtronic Ireland has constitutional standing, we reverse and remand.
14582: Article III standing: Spota, as assignee of the patent, retains an exclusionary right and has standing to sue; the district court's standing ruling is reversed as to Spota.
Accordingly, Spota has Article III standing and remains the patentee, entitled to sue for infringement.
14583: Standing for pre-assignment damages: Lowe lost standing to sue for infringement occurring before the December 9, 2021 assignment because he transferred all right to sue for past infringement.

Lowe lost standing on December 9, 2021, when he transferred his entire right, title and interest in the '664 patent, including the right to sue for past infringement during the time he owned the patent.
14629: Article III constitutional standing: whether the patent owner retained an exclusionary right (right to sue, sublicensing veto, royalty interests) after exclusively licensing rights to Ingevity, so as to have injury in fact.

On these facts, Plaintiff retained an exclusionary right sufficient for Article III standing, namely the non-illusory right to sue that their licensee, Ingevity, could not nullify through unilateral, royalty-free sublicensing.
14641: Standing to appeal: pro se appellants who did not personally sign the notices of appeal could not represent the other named plaintiffs, so those non-signing plaintiffs were not proper appellants.
pro se appellants must personally sign their notices of appeal.
14659: Standing to appeal: court declined to address the 102/103 portion of the appeal because the Board did not sustain those rejections and a party generally may not appeal from a favorable decision.
We therefore will not address that portion of Mr. McFadden's appeal because generally, a party may not appeal from a favorable decision.
14760: Standing: Rasmussen lacked Article III standing because it did not own the asserted patents when it filed suit.
we hold that Rasmussen lacked standing to bring its infringement suit because it did not own the Asserted Patents at the time that it filed its action
14775: Associational standing to challenge the PTO's denial of a petition for rulemaking under the APA and AIA; court held appellants lack associational standing because no member showed a non-speculative injury in fact.
We thus conclude that appellants lack associational standing.
14924: Standing: whether Oak Grove was an interested party with a substantial chance of award and was prejudiced
We affirm the Court of Federal Claims' denial of the government's motion to dismiss for lack of standing.
14991: Standing: the court held the Commission had standing to challenge the CIT's confidentiality order.

The Commission clearly has standing to challenge the order because disclosure of properly designated confidential business information could adversely affect the ability of the Commission to collect necessary information and to perform its statutory adjudicative functions.
15033: Standing: the court held the plaintiffs had Article III standing and that the trial court had jurisdiction, rejecting the lower court's standing dismissal while still affirming on the merits.
Hence, they established standing and that the Court of Federal Claims had subject matter jurisdiction.
15034: Organizational standing of MVA to challenge the Final Rule (injury-in-fact).
We hold MVA has organizational standing to challenge the Final Rule because MVA demonstrated injury-in-fact.
15058: Focus lacked standing to sue for infringement of the EZ ON mark because it did not own the mark when suit was filed; infringement finding reversed.
We therefore hold that Focus did not meet its burden to establish standing to sue Appellants for trademark infringement of the EZ ON mark.
15190: Standing: whether the non-lawyer plaintiff may represent the Tribe, and whether he may sue in his personal capacity under the Indian Tucker Act, which permits only a tribe, band, or identifiable group to sue.

the Indian Tucker Act by its terms provides that only an Indian tribe, band, or other identifiable group may seek relief under the Act, and that Mr. McCaster therefore could not bring an action under section 1505 in his personal capacity.
15285: Article III standing: AEG lacked a concrete stake because it could not bid due to the unchallenged PAL requirement and lacked a personal stake in the dispute
As such, "[b]ecause [AEG] ha[s] no concrete stake in the lawsuit, [it] lack[s] Article III standing."
15286: Tucker Act statutory standing: AEG was not an interested party with a direct economic interest or substantial chance of award, and was not prejudiced
We thus agree with the Claims Court that AEG lacks statutory standing under the Tucker Act.
